title: A lead form that notifies a person the same day
metaTitle: Notify a person the same day
excerpt: If the site promises a reply, notify a person the same day in a place they already watch. A form that lands in a mailbox nobody checks breaks the promise the button made.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases. A quiet room where someone still has to notice that a form arrived.
caption: A quiet room that still needs a person paying attention. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should happen after someone submits a lead form?
faqs.answer: A person who can reply should be notified the same day, in a channel or inbox they already open, with the name, the email, the page, and a link to the full note. The sender should see a confirmation that matches the promise beside the button. A database row nobody reads is not a finished form.

faqs.question: What does same day need to mean on the page?
faqs.answer: Define it. Business days, a cutoff, and a timezone are kinder than the word soon. If you cannot reply the same day, do not promise it. The notification's timestamp should make it obvious whether the window you published is still open.

faqs.question: How many fields should the form ask for?
faqs.answer: Ask for a name, an email, and what they want to talk about. Add a link or a budget range only if the person who is pinged will use it. A long quiz lowers the number of notes by turning away people who were ready to write, which is a quieter failure, not a better form.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Lead form notification is the system that makes a promise true. If the site says you will reply, a person has to know a submission arrived, the same day, in a place they already watch. A form that lands in a mailbox nobody checks is a broken promise, even when the database row is perfect.

The form is not done when it stores the fields. It is done when the right person can see them before the sender starts to wonder if the button worked.

## The promise and the ping are one feature

Write the promise in a sentence you can keep. “We reply within one business day.” “We reply the same day on business days.” Then design the notification to fire in time for that sentence. If your team only reads mail at 9 a.m., a same-day promise means the ping has to be visible before they leave, not buried in a digest at midnight.

Say the promise next to the button, and repeat it on the confirmation. The confirmation is part of the promise. “Sent. You’ll hear from us today.” If you cannot say today, do not say today. A softer true sentence beats a bold one you miss. People remember the miss longer than the form design.

Nielsen Norman Group’s article on [how long users stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/), from 2011, is about the first seconds on a page. The same impatience shows up after they submit. They gave you the hour they were going to spend deciding. Silence reads as a failure of the button, or as indifference. The notification is how your side of that moment stays awake.

Name a human owner of the inbox or the channel. A role is fine, “whoever is on leads this week,” if the calendar is real. A shared alias with no owner is how mail becomes archaeology. The owner can rotate. The rotation has to be written down.

## Where the notification should arrive

Send it to a place the person already opens during work. A chat channel they keep visible, or an inbox that is not also the inbox for newsletters and receipts. The worst destination is a tool they check “when they remember.” They will not remember on the day a founder wrote to you.

The message should contain enough to act, and no more than you want in that channel. Name, email, the page they submitted from, and the one-line reason they wrote. Link to the full record. Do not paste a long brief into a phone notification. Do paste the fact that lets someone see whether this is theirs.

Include the time and the timezone. “Arrived 3:10 p.m. Eastern” tells the owner whether the same-day promise still has hours left. A relative “just now” is useless in a log you read at 6.

If two people might reply, the notification should say who is responsible today. Two enthusiastic replies, or zero replies, are the failure modes of a shared ping with no owner. A simple convention works: the owner reacts when they have it, so the other person can see it is covered. Pick the convention and use it for a month before you buy a heavier tool.

Deduplicate. A double click should not create two emergencies. If the provider retries the webhook, the second delivery should not look like a second lead. Store a submission id and ignore the repeat, or mark it as a repeat in the message so nobody starts two threads.

## What the sender sees

The button should say what will happen. “Request a reply” is clearer than “Submit” if a reply is the promise. While the request is in flight, show a pending state. After success, replace the form with the confirmation sentence and what they sent, at least the email, so they can spot a typo.

Errors stay next to the field that failed. An email without an @, a required project URL, a message that exceeded a limit you forgot to mention. Say how to fix it. Do not clear the form on error. The [W3C’s WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treats understandable error recovery as part of a usable interface. A lead form is that kind of interface. Someone who cannot finish it will not become a lead, and they will not tell you why.

If the network fails after they typed, the confirmation must not claim you received it. “We could not send this. Your text is still here. Try again.” A cheerful thank-you on a failed post is a second broken promise in the same minute.

Spam and abuse filters should not eat a short, specific message from a real person. Test with a normal note, a note with a link, and a note that mentions a budget. If the legitimate one lands in junk on your side, fix the filter before you spend more time on the layout of the form. The sender did their part.

## The same day, in practice

Define “same day” on the page if you use the words. Business days, and the hours. “Same business day if you write before 4 p.m. Eastern. Otherwise the next business day.” That sentence is kinder than a vague “soon,” and it gives the notification a deadline you can see in the timestamp.

The owner needs a backup. If they are in a workshop, someone else is named, or the promise on the site changes for that day. A studio that disappears into a shoot and misses three inquiries has a staffing rule to write, not a form bug. The form can still ping a backup channel when the first reaction does not happen within a set number of hours. Keep that number inside the promise you published.

A reply can be short. It should come from a person, and it should answer the actual note. A template that ignores what they wrote is a notification in the other direction, and it feels automatic because it is. Use a template for the parts that never change, such as how to book a follow-up, and write the first lines yourself.

Do not auto-reply with a full proposal, a price, or a critique generated from their paragraph. You do not know enough yet. The safe automatic message is the confirmation you already showed on the page: we have it, a person will reply, here is the window. Anything smarter belongs to the person.

Log the first human reply time for a few weeks. You are looking for submissions that waited overnight without a reason. Those are the ones the notification missed, or the ones the owner saw and did not treat as the promise. Fix the path, not the adjective on the button.

## Fields that help the person who is pinged

Ask for what the reply needs, and nothing you will not read. A name, an email, what they want to talk about, and a link to the current site or product if they have one. A budget range can help if you truly use it to decide who replies. A twenty-field quiz will lower the number of pings by lowering the number of real senders. That is not efficiency. That is a quieter failure.

Optional fields should look optional. Required fields should be marked in text, not only by color. Phone number only if someone will call. Most studio conversations can start in writing. An obligatory phone field is how a careful founder abandons a form they were willing to complete.

Hidden fields are for you: the page URL, the campaign if you have one, the time. They belong in the notification so the owner has context. They do not belong as extra questions. UTM trivia is useful in the record and noisy in the sender’s face.

If you serve more than one kind of work, a single choice helps the route. “A marketing site, a product interface, or something else.” Three options. The notification can land in the same channel and still show the choice in the first line. A separate form per service is rarely worth the extra page at this stage.

Hanabi’s public work ranges from editorial sites such as Thomas Bewick to product interfaces such as Got Next and Leadly. The form does not need to diagnose which one a stranger resembles. It needs to carry their words to a person who can tell.

## Test the path the way they will use it

Submit from your phone, on the real site, to the real destination. Read the ping. Reply to yourself from the address the sender will see. Check the spam folder of the test inbox. Submit again with a missing field and read the error. Submit with the network offline if you can, and read that error too.

Then ask the owner, without warning, to find yesterday’s test. If they cannot, the notification is in the wrong place. Move it before you restyle the form.

After a lead is real, the work turns into decisions a builder has to see. [Handoff notes between design and build](/blog/handoff-notes-between-design-and-build) is the next piece, because a fast reply that starts a project still fails if the notes between design and engineering leave the states unspoken.

If the form on your site is still a placeholder, the implementation sits with the rest of the marketing site in [Hanabi’s services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful version is the one a person is pinged about the same day.
